title: Bug Hotel & Wormery
strapline: Homes for minibeasts we build and tend — learning to look closely, care gently and understand how tiny things live.
intent: Children build a genuine, caring relationship with living creatures, learning to handle and protect them gently.
Children observe minibeasts closely over time — where they live, what they eat, how they move — real, patient science.
Children understand life cycles, habitats and decomposition through creatures they can watch day after day.
Children develop responsibility, tending a home for living things that depend on their care.
Children build vocabulary and curiosity — questioning, describing and classifying the creatures they find.
implementation: Build the bug hotel together from real materials — pallets, bamboo, pine cones, bark, straw, drilled logs — each layer a different creature's home.
Set up a wormery in a clear container so children can watch worms tunnelling, mixing soil and turning scraps to compost over weeks.
Teach gentle handling from the outset: soft hands, watch don't squash, and always return creatures to where they were found.
Provide the tools of a scientist — magnifiers, bug pots, spotting cards, a clipboard — so looking closely becomes the habit.
Feed and tend it as a real responsibility — worm food, keeping the wormery moist, checking the hotel — shared among the children.
Talk it through and record it: which creatures moved in, what worms eat, what changed — building understanding over the seasons.
key_questions: Which creature do you think lives in this part of the hotel?
How should we hold the minibeast to keep it safe?
What are the worms doing to the soil and scraps?
Where do you think this bug likes to live, and why?
What does our wormery need to stay healthy?

impact.text: Children treat living things gently as a matter of course and expect others to.
Children show care for creatures — gentle hands, quiet feet, tending their home.
Children watch living things with fascination and learn how they live and change.
Children ask real questions about the world and expect real answers.
Children sort, match and notice same and different among the creatures they find.

enhancements: A minibeast identification wall with photos and children's own drawings of who they've spotted.
A composting link — kitchen scraps to the wormery, worm compost to the growing patch — closing a real cycle.
A life-cycle focus — caterpillars to butterflies, or frog spawn — watched and recorded over weeks.
A 'minibeast hospital' role-play corner where found creatures are gently cared for and released.
A seasonal audit — who's home in the bug hotel in spring versus winter?

playing_exploring: Children explore the hidden world of minibeasts up close, following their fascination.
Hunting for and observing creatures invites open, hands-on investigation.
active_learning: Tending the creatures over time builds genuine responsibility and persistence.
Children return again and again to check on 'their' worms and bugs.
creating_thinking: Children ask questions, make predictions and reason about how creatures live.
They connect habitat, food and life cycle, building real understanding.
